tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: ShowOnboardingRolePicker
tools.description:
Render a clickable role-picker chip row during Cowork onboarding. Call this when asking the user what kind of work they do so they can pick their role and get a matching plugin installed. The role list is hardcoded in the frontend — call with no args.

The call blocks until the user responds. Do NOT call this in normal conversation. Only call this when explicitly helping the user set up Cowork for their role/job function.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly.     name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

376

378	
379	1. **Current claim and scope.** What is established, on which execution path, library, call form or other relevant conditions. The title must not imply a broader claim than the body supports.
380	2. **Consequence and limits.** What a worker can safely conclude or do, with exceptions and unresolved uncertainty kept beside the claim. Include consequences only when they matter.

384

393	| Scope | Title and body agree on the path, conditions and limits; the statement does not generalize beyond its support. |
394	| Present meaning | The reader can identify the current property, or the explicitly bounded historical observation, without reconstructing a batch's work. |
395	| Evidence | The stated support can be found and supports the retained claim; uncertainty and the kind of evidence are accurately represented. |
396	| Comprehension | Given normal language prerequisites, a reader can restate the finding and its consequence. Subjects, referents and technical terms are unambiguous. |
397	| Ownership | The entry has one independently maintainable subject; unrelated repairs, chronology and duplicated current counts do not obscure it. |
398	| Consistency | Relevant linked or same-subject entries agree, or their different scopes or unresolved conflict are explicit. |

405	- **Reword:** supported meaning is sound, but presentation or scope wording fails.

- **Record pass:** produce the final readable entries and check their scope, evidence and related statements. The coordinator's instructions assign this to the batch commit stage, and to the coordinator after a lone worker.
- **Coordinator:** own the guidance and verify that the pass occurred. Delegate the writing through the existing process; this need not become another task the coordinator personally performs in full.

Align the rung brief's request for “finished prose” with the worker skill: request complete findings, while making the record pass responsible for final editorial wording.

Put the schema clarification and assessment criteria in `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`. Ensure the actual batch stage brief carries that guidance, rather than assuming the descriptive skill text alone causes it to happen. The full pass is a one-time repair of the accumulated record; subsequent landings apply the same criteria to new, changed and affected related entries. Do not add another full-record audit after every landing.

For routine acceptance, keep the central question short:

> Can a reader identify what is established, under which conditions, and what it means for the work, without reconstructing what the batch changed?

The corresponding POSITIONS question remains about faithful communication of the curator's ruling. The shared register helps both; their evidence and ownership requirements remain distinct.

## Review limits

This review sampled Revival and its sources. It did not reread the whole file, audit FACTS or POSITIONS, inspect transcripts, run builds, or test the numerical claims anew. Growth measurements are attributed to the existing scout report.

<!-- The clarity workflow: rewrite POSITIONS or FACTS entries so that each reads on its own, with a cold read and a fidelity check, as a Workflow run; how to run it and what to do with its output. -->

# The clarity workflow

`record-clarity.js` rewrites record entries so that a reader who knows the language, but never saw the conversation or the batch behind an entry, can tell what it says. It is the process of the clarity pilot of 2026-10-22 (`positions-audit/clarity/`, ten POSITIONS entries, approved and applied at `6b560762f`), run as a Workflow, in the shape of the `fortress-repo` skill rewrite of 2026-10-08 (Workflow run `wf_185878c8-0fb`: writers, cold readers, a fix round). Its standard is Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`.

## What runs, for each chunk of about ten entries

1. **Assess** (FACTS only): Astra's rubric over every entry (`assess.md`); a disposition each: keep, reword, reorganize or investigate. Only reword and reorganize go on.
2. **Write**: the stream's headless Opus writer (`writer-stream.sh`, the skill writer's standing brief) with `writer.md`. For POSITIONS its evidence is the provenance audit's, by `entries.py`; for FACTS, the assessment and each entry's cited sources. A Sonnet step only runs the command and waits (`wait.py`).
3. **Cold read**: an Opus reader with only the `fortress-repo` skill's core and area parts, never its revival part (`coldread.md`).
4. **Check**: fidelity against the sources, and the reader's answers against the source meaning (`check.md`).
5. **Fix**: the writer's second round (`fix.md`), in the same stream, so it resumes the session that wrote the chunk with its evidence in the cache.
6. **Reread**: a second cold read of the fixed entries.
7. **Judge**: once, per entry, apply or hold (`judge.md`), so that no chunk loops; it writes `final.apply` and `queue.md`.

**The writer stream.** One headless Opus session per Workflow run takes its chunks in turn (`flock`), resumed while its context stays under 400K tokens written and its cache is warm (under 50 minutes idle), and started fresh otherwise. In the pilot its fix round wrote 61K tokens, where a fresh writer would read everything again. A Workflow runs at most two agents at once on this machine: run several side by side, each with its own stream.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/record-clarity.js',
               args: { kind: 'positions' | 'facts', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'name', chunks: [{ name: 'c1', entries: ['P-7', 'P-8'] }] } })

`from: 'judge'` runs only the judge, on chunks written before the judge existed.

Each chunk's files land in `out` + its name: `proposals.md`, `clean.txt`, `proposals.apply`, `concepts.md`, `cold-read.md`, `check.md`, `cold-read-2.md`, `judgement.md`, `final.apply`, `queue.md`, the writer's logs, and for FACTS `assessment.md`. Resume a killed run with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte.

## After a chunk

The coordinator's part is mechanical:
- apply the judge's `final.apply` on a copy of the record, `record.py check --base`, then on `main`, and commit the record with the chunk's files;
- file `queue.md` in `review-queue.md` (a worker, for several chunks at once);
- merge `concepts.md` into the concepts list that the orientation workflow reads.

POSITIONS entries need the provenance audit's evidence first: for entries it has not traced, run the mining workflow (`positions-audit/README.md`).

# FACTS chunk f0: the rewrite

The base is `main` at `df0728b81`, as in `assessment.md`; the fix round read at `30ee7ae4b`, whose library, ledger and gate files are the base's (`check.md`). The assessment keeps F-261 and F-262, so this file holds the other three: F-151 (reword), F-263 and F-264 (reorganize). Each entry's sources are the assessment's and the check's citations, read again for the sentence that cites them. A section number is that of the report named. Concepts that the entries use and that every worker needs are in `concepts.md`.

The fix round changed what `check.md` marks, and the readings that `cold-read.md` could not resolve:
- F-151: which declarations need `Number`'s exclusion, corrected; the library named; the default's wording; the plain array said as a run-time result; two claims added from the sources.
- F-263: the compiled path's negative power narrowed to `ZZ32`'s and its bases; the `IntLiteral` value, the exponent beyond 64 bits and row 523's failure said plainly.
- F-264: the subscripts' cast put back on the sub-array that they pass to `Col` and `Row`; the walk claim at landing narrowed to its measurement; the factory branches and the five bodies that need no cast named.

The three entries hold 3,179 characters in the record and 5,905 here: F-151 617 to 1,850, F-263 1,359 to 1,962, F-264 1,203 to 2,093. The growth is the words that say what each pointer holds, the names that replace the batches' short forms, the conditions that the old text left to the reader, and the fix round's corrections and named lists. `record.py apply` of `proposals.apply` on a scratch clone of the record at `30ee7ae4b`, then `record.py check --base df0728b81` on it: 0 failures.

## F-151

> - F-151 **In the interpreter's library, `Vector`, `Matrix` and their factories and operators bound their element type by `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.** `Number` declares no arithmetic, so the compiled checker accepts the bodies' arithmetic only through `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`. `Number` stays in the bound because its `comprises` clause lists every type below it, so an element type excludes `String`; the ring alone does not give that. That exclusion makes the four juxtapositions of a vector or a matrix with a scalar `T`, in either order, a valid overloading beside the library's juxtapositions with a `String`. `Number` also declares the `asFloat` that the vector norm calls. The eight number types meet the bound. `Number` itself and the numeral type `IntLiteral` do not, since neither is a ring at its own type. So `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not a well-formed type, and `array1` and `array2` have no branch for `Number`: called at `Number`, they give a plain array at run time, not a vector or a matrix (F-229). POSITIONS.md:37
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. Wherever the array design creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. Each builds its result with the inherited `map` or `ivmap`, typed `Array1` or `Array2`, and so through `replica`, the method that makes an array of the same layout. The factory branches are those of `__builtinFactory1`, `__immutableFactory1` and `__builtinFactory2` for an array whose lowest indices are 0, each cast to its factory's declared result type. The subscripts are `a[:, j]` and `a[i, :]`. # Rung G, climb batch 6.5: generics at run time on the compiled path

problem: six compiled-path failures, each re-captured on the base before any edit: row 417's first-load race at four threads (explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/threads-before.txt:10), row 419's task (probes/junit-before.txt:128), row 420 (:151), the renamed-arm and ZZ32 dispatch defects (:71, :109), row 351 at the typecase and catch sites (:6, :174) and row 426 through the compiler library's cast (explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/junit-before.txt:25)
spec: dispatch to the most specific declaration applicable at run time, Specification/basic/overloading.tex:262-276, with one instantiation fixed at the call (:100-107, :136-138); static parameters in scope in the entire body, Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:19-24, and each `also` block in its own thread, Specification/basic/expressions/also.tex:17-21; the catch value bound to the identifier, Specification/basic/expressions/try.tex:56-60; the typecase value bound and matched by subtype, Specification/basic/expressions/typecase.tex:88-99, with `cast` defined by it, Specification/basic/expressions/casting.tex:15-34
precedent: row 419 copies forFnExpr's own closure device (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3479-3489); row 351 copies forLocalVarDecl's local and nested scope (:3959-3962, :4018-4027) and conditionallyCastParameter's cast (:6463-6467); row 417 takes the lock of the JDK method it overrides (explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/jdk-loadclass-javap.txt:2-9), the team's check-again-under-the-table's-lock (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/RttiTupleMap.java:148-157); the dispatch change is the measured patch (explorations/compile-ladder/plan-6.5/probes/dispatch/callsite-rebased.patch:1-119)
deviation: the dispatch patch without its `-Dprobe.scope` switch and its `skip` variant (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:1338-1370); row 419's patch plus the deletion of the TO DO line it answers (CodeGen.java:1633); the lock wraps the old body in a helper rather than re-indenting it, and `history` is still written before `defineClass` (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178-211); the identity functions' ZZ32 and RR64 branches take a typed binding where the answer-7 text passed a numeral (Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3126-3128)
historical: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178-185, ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1633-1638, :2059-2061, :2131-2137, :2156-2164, :4785-4817, ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:41, :58, :1338-1370, :1395-1431, :1817-1821, Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3126-3156

Every capture named below is in `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/` unless a path says otherwise. The harness refused this rung's write of this file; the gather writes it from the structured result.

## 1. What is fixed

All six, on the compiled path:

1. **Row 417, the first-load race.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` now runs under `getClassLoadingLock(name)`, the lock the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` takes and this override had dropped. `FirstLoadThreadsRungG` fails 5 of 5 compiled runs at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4` on the base (`threads-before.txt:10-14`, `NullPointerException ... "cl" is null`) and passes 5 of 5 after (`threads-after.txt:10-14`); both pass at one thread. Rung Z's `ZsThreadsT`, `ZsThreadsS`, `ZsThreads` and the control `ZsThreadsLit` pass 5 of 5 at both counts (`threads-zs-after.txt`), and a 24-instantiation widening passes 5 of 5 (`FirstLoad24.fss`, `threads-24-after.txt`).
2. **Row 419, a task in a generic declaration.** The measured 13-line patch: `delegate` makes the task class generic over the task's free static parameters, as `forFnExpr` does for a closure. `NatRtTask` (promoted from `XXXNatRtTask`) passes.
3. **Row 420, a generic method building over two parameter sets.** Its site is row 419's: the method's `||` operands are run as a task, and the task class was not generic. Disassembled on the base, the method template `H☝m⟦☝,U,T⟧` builds its second operand in the non-generic `ZrMethNoClosureT$task0`, which names `U`. Two controls on the base settle it (`row420-cause-before.txt`): the method's own parameter alone, in two task operands, fails the same way (`MethOneParTask`, `U$RTTIc`), and both parameters with no task operand pass (`MethBothNoTask`, `stringzz32`). Row 419's fix closes it: `NatRtMethBoth` (promoted, with a third assertion for `MethOneParTask`'s shape) passes. The row's "both parameters" reading was the controls' shape, not the cause.
4. **A generic arm naming its static parameters differently from its template dispatcher.** The measured call-site change. `DispatchRenamedArmRungG` and `DispatchSwappedArmRungG` (the plan's `ScopeArmsLegal` and `ScopeAlpha2`) pass.
5. **A `ZZ32` instantiation spelled at run time.** Avoided on template dispatchers by the same change, which names the arm at the dispatcher's own parameters instead of reading them off the value. `DispatchZZ32ArmRungG` (`ScopeZZ32Sub`) passes. The two spellings remain (section 9).
6. **Row 351, a clause's bound name, and row 426.** `forTypecase` binds a named clause's value as a local for the clause body, and `forTry` binds the catch name the same way. `TypecaseBindRungG`, `ArrowClauseBindRungG` (`andCondCombine`'s shape), `CastBindRungG`, `WitnessIdentityRungG` and `ClauseBindingRungB` (promoted from `XXXClauseBindingRungB`) pass. Row 426 was row 351: the compiled `cast[\T\]` matched and then read its clause name as a missing top-level object. `cast-template-javap.txt` shows it: before, `getstatic fortress/CompilerLibrary$y.ONLY` (`:11`); after, `checkcast T`, `astore_1`, `aload_1` (`:35-37`). Its numeral half, `cast[\ZZ32\](0)` throwing, is the specification's answer (section 4). Answer 7's identity functions now pass values of type `T` through `cast` in their `ZZ32` and `RR64` branches. A named clause or a `catch` inside a `do … also` arm whose body then reads a captured variable still fails verification. A local in a task body takes `this`'s slot (row 497). A `catch` there also meets row 322's mechanism (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/skeptic/clause-in-task.txt:33-34`, `:50`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/skeptic/clause-in-task-split.txt:62`, `:95`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/skeptic/try-in-arm.txt:41`).

What remains is recorded, not fixed: the dispatch change's remainder (generic dotted methods, home 2; a dispatcher that is not a template, home 3), sections 9 and 10.

## 12. Decisions, each with the ways not taken

- **The lock's shape.** Candidates:
  - `synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name))` around the whole of `loadClass`, which is the loader's own monitor. Taken.
  - The same with `registerAsParallelCapable`, one lock per name.
  - A lock only in `loadClosureClass`.
  - A `ConcurrentHashMap` of futures per name.

  The monitor is the lock the JVM already holds when it resolves a class through a loader that is not parallel-capable, and it is what the JDK's own `loadClass` takes. Explicit loads (`loadClosureClass`, `getRTTIclass`, the union instantiation) were the only ones running without it. Taking it adds no lock order the implicit loads do not already have: a generation step that initialises another class under the monitor, as `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:274` can, already does so on every implicit load. Per-name locks would admit two loads each holding one name's lock while generating a class that needs the other's; the JDK leaves them off unless a loader opts in. A lock in `loadClosureClass` alone leaves the other two explicit callers racing. Futures would change the loader's structure for no gain the measurement can see.
- **Where `history` is written.** Left before `defineClass`. Under the lock no other thread can see the name before its class is defined. Moving the write would change what the same thread does if generation re-enters the loader for the name it is generating, which it does not today by reading, and every single-thread run would need re-measuring for no gain. The pre-existing behaviour after a failed load, where the name stays in `history` and a later load of it returns null (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:189-193`), is unchanged; by reading, not measured.
- **Binding a catch name always.** The grammar makes the name mandatory (`try.tex:22`), and the specification binds it (`:56-60`), so every catch clause's code changes: `getValue`, a cast and a store in place of a pop. The prelude has no `catch`, so no library class moves. The other way, binding only a name the body reads, needs a free-variable test at each clause and saves three instructions.
- **Binding a typecase clause's name only when it has one.** Clauses without a name pop as before, which is why only `cast`'s template changed in the prelude.
- **The identity functions' values of type `T`.** Two ways were on file:
  - A typed binding, `v: ZZ32 = 0` then `cast[\T\](v)`, which converts a numeral by coercion on the compiled path and keeps walk's value as it is (FACTS.md, "Under walk, the interpreter converts by coercion at its three kinds of type check", FACTS.md:110). Taken, in the two branches that passed a numeral.
  - A checker refinement that binds `T` inside a witness branch (`explorations/reviews/sum-replacement-judgement.md` section 7, check 3), which is Scala and not this rung's. Not taken.

  `typed` would not do: the compiled path has no `forAsExpr`. The six branches that pass a function's result (`widen`, `unsigned`, `big`, `Ratio`, `narrow`) are unchanged. They have values of their type under walk, where a numeral is a `ZZ32`, and in the compiled checker's reading of the one library, where `IntLiteral` extends `ZZ32` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:117`). They do not over the compiled prelude, where a numeral reaches `ZZ32`'s and `NN32`'s `widen` by coercion alone and the checker's pick differed between two compiles (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5/merged-review/witness-identity-gate.txt`, `compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5/judge-repair/witness-suite-javap.txt`). So `WitnessIdentityRungG` widens a typed `ZZ32` since the judge's repair (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5/JUDGE-review.md` section 2).
- **Row 420's fix is row 419's.** No separate edit was made; the row closes with 419, its cause located and gated.
- **Home 3, not home 2, for a dispatcher that is not a template.** The batch record plans home 2 for both remainders "where the rung shows it failing" (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.5.md:188`). For generic dotted methods the rung took it (`XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG`). For a dispatcher that is not a template the alternative was an `XXX` test asserting only that the call does not throw and answers one of the two declarations. It was not taken, because the chapter as committed forbids the pair (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:102-105`), so no passage says which answer a test should hold, and the grep of section 9 finds none; home 3, the probes and row 496.
- **Two more compiled tests than the brief named.** `WitnessIdentityRungG` is answer 7's identity shape in the compiler's world. It is the judgement's check 3, `zeroOf[\RR64\]()` through a repaired `cast`, now gated. `XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG` is the remainder's home 2.

Two controls on the base settle it (`row420-cause-before.txt`): the method's own parameter alone, in two task operands, fails the same way (`MethOneParTask`, `U$RTTIc`), and both parameters with no task operand pass (`MethBothNoTask`, `stringzz32`). 6. **Row 351, a clause's bound name, and row 426.** `forTypecase` binds a named clause's value as a local for the clause body, and `forTry` binds the catch name the same way. `TypecaseBindRungG`, `ArrowClauseBindRungG` (`andCondCombine`'s shape), `CastBindRungG`, `WitnessIdentityRungG` and `ClauseBindingRungB` (promoted from `XXXClauseBindingRungB`) pass. Row 426 was row 351: the compiled `cast[\T\]` matched and then read its clause name as a missing top-level object. `cast-template-javap.txt` shows it: before, `getstatic fortress/CompilerLibrary$y.ONLY` (`:11`); after, `checkcast T`, `astore_1`, `aload_1` (`:35-37`). Its numeral half, `cast[\ZZ32\](0)` throwing, is the specification's answer (section 4). Answer 7's identity functions now pass values of type `T` through `cast` in their `ZZ32` and `RR64` branches. ## 12. Decisions, each with the ways not taken

- **The lock's shape.** Candidates:
  - `synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name))` around the whole of `loadClass`, which is the loader's own monitor. Taken.
  - The same with `registerAsParallelCapable`, one lock per name.
  - A lock only in `loadClosureClass`.
  - A `ConcurrentHashMap` of futures per name.

  The monitor is the lock the JVM already holds when it resolves a class through a loader that is not parallel-capable, and it is what the JDK's own `loadClass` takes. Explicit loads (`loadClosureClass`, `getRTTIclass`, the union instantiation) were the only ones running without it. Taking it adds no lock order the implicit loads do not already have: a generation step that initialises another class under the monitor, as `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:274` can, already does so on every implicit load. Per-name locks would admit two loads each holding one name's lock while generating a class that needs the other's; the JDK leaves them off unless a loader opts in. A lock in `loadClosureClass` alone leaves the other two explicit callers racing. Futures would change the loader's structure for no gain the measurement can see.
- **Where `history` is written.** Left before `defineClass`. Under the lock no other thread can see the name before its class is defined. Moving the write would change what the same thread does if generation re-enters the loader for the name it is generating, which it does not today by reading, and every single-thread run would need re-measuring for no gain. The pre-existing behaviour after a failed load, where the name stays in `history` and a later load of it returns null (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:189-193`), is unchanged; by reading, not measured.
- **Binding a catch name always.** The grammar makes the name mandatory (`try.tex:22`), and the specification binds it (`:56-60`), so every catch clause's code changes: `getValue`, a cast and a store in place of a pop. The prelude has no `catch`, so no library class moves. The other way, binding only a name the body reads, needs a free-variable test at each clause and saves three instructions.
- **Binding a typecase clause's name only when it has one.** Clauses without a name pop as before, which is why only `cast`'s template changed in the prelude.
- **The identity functions' values of type `T`.** Two ways were on file:

Taken, in the two branches that passed a numeral.
  - A checker refinement that binds `T` inside a witness branch (`explorations/reviews/sum-replacement-judgement.md` section 7, check 3), which is Scala and not this rung's. Not taken.

  `typed` would not do: the compiled path has no `forAsExpr`. The six branches that pass a function's result (`widen`, `unsigned`, `big`, `Ratio`, `narrow`) are unchanged. They have values of their type under walk, where a numeral is a `ZZ32`, and in the compiled checker's reading of the one library, where `IntLiteral` extends `ZZ32` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:117`). For generic dotted methods the rung took it (`XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG`). f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\]): ZZ32 = v.x

end

  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or

  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's

  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first

  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose

  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such

11	## 1. What changed
12	
13	Walk's test harness reads a key that names a refusal at load. Three things change in walk's load check.
14	
15	- **The key.** A file `Name.fss` of `ProjectFortress/tests/` names the refusal at load it expects in `Name.test` beside it, in the compiled tests' format: `load_exception_contains=<text>`, or any other `load_` key that `generalTestFailed` reads. A plain test passes when walk refuses the program at load with an exception that meets the key. An `XXX` test is the expected failure of that: it passes when the program loads and runs without an exception and without `fail` or `FAIL` in its output. It fails when walk refuses it as the key names, or when it fails in any other way (`FileTests.java:456-515`, `:835-879`).
16	- **Row 552.** The overlap reading of a generic declaration beside a plain one now handles every shape of static parameter:
17	  - a type parameter with several bounds is read as the intersection of its bounds;
18	  - a bound that names a static parameter is left out;
19	  - a parameter type that mentions a static parameter is read as `Any`;
20	  - a non-type static parameter is no longer a reason to refuse.
21

## 2. The count

### The mechanisms

- `builtinPrimitive` bodies: 425 live bindings in nine files. 20 more sit inside comments (`FortressBuiltin.fss:501-537`, 19; `FortressLibrary.fss:4338`, 1); the record's 231 and 126 per file count them.
- Objects of a `native component`, whose Java class walk loads by name (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildNativeEnvironment.java:42-47`): 32.
- Names walk binds at start-up: `true`, `false`, `Any` (`interpreter/evaluator/Primitives.java:38-52`).

Counted at `f55fd68e2`. Recounted on `main` at `e455ccd98`, after rung V made `RR32` a sibling of `RR64` (`git show` copies under a private directory, the same scripts): 424 live, one `RR32` binding of class C fewer, nothing else moved.

Matched against the compiler prelude's 366 declarations whose bodies call an `import java` alias (`CompilerBuiltin.fss` 364, `CompilerLibrary.fss` 1, `CompilerSystem.fss` 1), over 369 public static helpers in 25 classes (`natives-shape/helpers-javap.txt`). Matching is by owner, name and signature, the owner mapped between the two spellings (`Int` and `ZZ32` to `ZZ32`, `Float` to `RR64`, `Char` to `Character`, `FlatString` to `JavaString`), and then by operation: each glue class to the helper that computes the same thing. Scripts: `natives-shape/count/extract.py`, `match.py`, `classify.py`; every binding's class is in `count/classified.tsv`.

### The classes

- **A, bound, 147.** The compiler prelude binds the same operation at the same owner and signature. Only the binding text changes.
- **B, helper exists, 61.** A helper computes it; nothing binds it under this name and signature yet.
- **C, new helper, 139.** A static helper over Java values must be written; the glue class's body is its source.
- **D1, native I/O object, 36.** A method of `Writer`, `BufferedWriter`, `FileReadStream`, `FileWriteStream` or `Reader`. It needs a Java-backed type in the one library, as the compiler prelude's `JavaBufferedReader`/`Writer` (`NamingCzar.java:449-450`), then helpers; `fileOps` already has 17 over them.
- **D2, no compiled analogue, 42.** Reflection, `Thread`, the native arrays, the task trace.

### By file

- `FortressBuiltin.fss`, 212: A 88, B 23, C 96, D2 5 (`Thread`).
- `FortressLibrary.fss`, 125: A 56, B 31, C 37, D2 1 (`printTaskTrace`).
- `Reflect.fss`, 28: D2 28.
- `File.fss`, 15: D1 15.
- `FlatString.fss`, 14: A 2, B 7, C 5.
- `Writer.fss`, 11: D1 11.
- `Reader.fss`, 10: D1 10.
- `NativeArray.fss`, 7: D2 7.
- `System.fss`, 3: A 1 (`getProperty`), C 1 (`getEnvironment`), D2 1 (`getProgramArgsPrim`).

The prelude and what it imports (`FortressBuiltin`, `FortressLibrary`, `FlatString`, `Writer`, `NativeArray`) hold 369 of the 425: A 146, B 61, C 138, D1 11, D2 13. The other 56 load only when a program imports `Reflect`, `File`, `Reader` or `System`.

### What the classes hide

- **Same name, other meaning.** 25 of B carry a name the compiler prelude binds to another helper. 12 are the wrapping operators: the one library binds `DOTPLUS` to wrapping addition (`FortressLibrary.fss:718`), the compiler prelude to saturating addition (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:676`), ledger row 348. Copying the compiler prelude's binding would be wrong for them.
- **Parameters that are not Java values.** 37 bindings take `AnyIntegral` (17), `Type` (11), `Any` (5), `Number` (3), `T` (3) or a function (4): B 10, C 11, D2 16. The body converts before the call, or the helper takes a Fortress type.
- **The size of C.** 132 distinct glue classes, 0.7K lines of glue Java, median 5 lines each. `RR32` 50 (no float helper exists but `floatToDouble`), `Float` 28 (directed rounding, raw bits, NaN tests), the integer families' `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `partitionL`, `^`, `CHOOSE`, shifts and conversions 42 (the compiler prelude writes the first four in Fortress, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:686-705`), the literals 8, strings and `StringPrim` 10, `nanoTime` 1 (the compiled one returns `RR64`).
- **Every program's output is D1.** `println` writes through `stdOut` (`FortressLibrary.fss:4246-4249`), a native `Writer` object (`Library/Writer.fss:20-24`). The first compiled program on the one library needs `Writer`'s natives.
- **microGPT's path.** It calls `nanoTime` (C) and imports `System` (`explorations/apl/microgpt/MicroGptApl.fss:16`), whose top-level `args` calls `getProgramArgsPrim` (D2) when the component loads (`Library/System.fss:28`). Its arrays reach `NativeArray` (D2).
- **Native objects.** Of the 32, the compiled path has a run-time value class for 12 (`compiler/runtimeValues/`: `FRR64`, `FRR32`, `FFloatLiteral`, `FZZ32`, `FZZ64`, `FNN32`, `FNN64`, `FIntLiteral`, `FZZ`, `FBoolean`, `FCharacter`, `FJavaString`), an analogue for the 5 I/O objects (`FortressBufferedReader`/`Writer`), and nothing for 15 (`Thread`, the 3 arrays, the 11 `Reflect` objects).
